source_evidence.anchor: Equation (1) and the paragraph defining stable matrix multiplication
source_evidence.observation: For exact n-by-n operands with C = A B, stability means that the computed C_comp satisfies ||C_comp-C|| <= mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B|| + O(epsilon^2). Epsilon is machine epsilon, and mu(n) is a low-degree polynomial O(n^c). The authors explicitly permit changing norms at the cost of additional dimension-dependent factors.

source_evidence.anchor: Paragraph interpreting normwise backward stability after equation (1)
source_evidence.observation: The paper states that O(epsilon) notation may absorb a factor n^c for a modest constant c.

source_evidence.anchor: Opening of Section 3, condition-number and backward-stability definitions
source_evidence.observation: The surrounding framework is perturbative: condition numbers and forward errors are expanded to first order, with quadratic perturbation terms represented by big-O terms.

source_evidence.anchor: Definition 3.1 and the opening block formula in Section 3.1
source_evidence.observation: Logarithmic stability is defined through a relative error of first order in epsilon, plus O(epsilon^2). Recursive triangular inversion uses the exact block identity whose off-diagonal block is -T11^(-1) T12 T22^(-1).

source_evidence.anchor: Paragraph beginning 'To show that this algorithm is logarithmically stable' and equation (8)
source_evidence.observation: The authors explicitly call the analysis first order and call err(T^(-1),n) an absolute error. For C = A B with inherited operand errors, equation (8) prints the three terms mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B||, ||A|| err(B,n), and err(A,n) ||B||.

source_evidence.anchor: Paragraph and recurrences immediately following equation (8)
source_evidence.observation: The recursive proof defines err(n') as a bound on normwise inverse error, applies equation (8) using inequalities, uses ||Tii|| <= ||T|| and ||Tii^(-1)|| <= ||T^(-1)||, and chooses to form T11^(-1) T12 before multiplying by T22^(-1).

source_evidence.anchor: Final triangular-inversion recurrence and its solution
source_evidence.observation: The first-order product rule yields an error recurrence bounded by 2(kappa(T)+1) err(n/2) + 2 mu(n/2) epsilon kappa(T) ||T^(-1)|| and hence an O(mu(n/2) epsilon kappa(T) [2(kappa(T)+1)]^(log_2 n) ||T^(-1)||) bound.

Equation (8) is reused for products in the distinct dense-inversion algorithm, including a case with no inherited error in one operand. This later analysis explicitly specializes its norm to the 2-norm.

binders: n is the local order of the square product C = A B; equation (1) introduces A, B, and C as n-by-n square matrices, while recursive calls use local order n/2. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: recurrences after equation (8)]

A and B are the reference operands for the product C = A B, and err(A,n) and err(B,n) represent errors inherited by their computed approximations from prior computations. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: sentence introducing equation (8)]

In the enclosing application, T is an invertible n-by-n upper block-triangular matrix with n/2-by-n/2 diagonal blocks T11 and T22 and off-diagonal block T12. [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: recursive triangular-inverse block formula and following dimension sentence]

epsilon is the working machine epsilon, and mu(n) is the dimension-dependent stability factor of the selected multiplication algorithm. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: paragraph following equation (1)]
hypotheses: The matrix-multiplication routine satisfies the normwise stability bound (1) for exact square operands. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1)]
The product invocation may receive operands carrying errors from earlier computations. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: sentence introducing equation (8)]

Equation (8) is used in a first-order perturbation regime; inherited errors are therefore treated as first-order quantities in epsilon, although the paper does not separately state err(A,n)=O(epsilon) and err(B,n)=O(epsilon) as formal hypotheses. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: 'we do a first order error analysis' and equation (8)]

The norm must support triangle-inequality and product-error propagation; the triangular proof additionally assumes diagonal-submatrix monotonicity with the displayed unit constants. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8) and the paragraph beginning 'We will also use the facts']
For the recursive triangular-inversion application, the required inverses T^(-1), T11^(-1), and T22^(-1) exist. [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: block inverse formula]
conclusions: The printed rule is err(C,n) = mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B|| + ||A|| err(B,n) + err(A,n) ||B||. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]

Its three retained contributions are, respectively, fresh roundoff from matrix multiplication, amplification of B's inherited error by ||A||, and amplification of A's inherited error by ||B||. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: annotations beside the three lines of equation (8)]

Despite the printed equality sign, equation (8) is not an exact identity for actual error matrices or error norms. In context it is a first-order error budget used as an upper bound, modulo omitted higher-order terms; the subsequent applications use <= and describe bounds. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence, equation (8), and following recurrences]

In recursive triangular inversion, systematic application of this local rule to the two products in -T11^(-1) T12 T22^(-1) produces the recurrence and logarithmic-stability bound stated on the following page. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed 66-67), anchor: recurrences following equation (8) and their solution]
definitions_and_conventions: err(X,n) is a scalar absolute normwise error quantity or bound for the computed version of X at local dimension n, not a perturbation matrix. The later err(n') notation is explicitly a bound applying to any encountered n'-by-n' diagonal inverse block. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis paragraph and definition of err(n')]

In equation (1), C = A B is exact and C_comp is computed. Equation (8) suppresses computed-value decorations and records their effects through err(A,n), err(B,n), and err(C,n). [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]
epsilon is machine epsilon and bounds roundoff error. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: sentence following equation (1)]
mu(n) is a low-degree polynomial in n: mu(n)=O(n^c) for some constant c. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: sentence following equation (1)]
For triangular inversion, kappa(T)=||T|| ||T^(-1)||, and the proof similarly defines kappa(Tii)=||Tii|| ||Tii^(-1)||. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: paragraph after equation (8)]

Big-O error notation is asymptotic in epsilon and may absorb polynomial factors in dimension under the paper's standing convention. [PDF p. 3 (printed 61), anchor: interpretation of O(epsilon); PDF p. 6 (printed 64), anchor: perturbative condition-number expansion]
implicit_context: The unadorned A and B in equation (8) function as reference values, while their computed approximations carry the stated inherited errors; equation (8) does not formally introduce perturbations Delta A and Delta B. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: sentence introducing equation (8)]

For fixed matrices and dimension, the recursive error quantities remain first order in epsilon because the recurrence is linear in inherited error and is driven by terms proportional to epsilon. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed 66-67), anchor: triangular-inversion error recurrences and final bound]

The recursive formula presumes repeated halving into equal blocks, but Section 3.1 does not state an odd-dimension convention, padding rule, or explicit power-of-two hypothesis. [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: block formula and n/2 dimension sentence]

No real-only or complex-only scalar domain is stated for equation (1), equation (8), or recursive triangular inversion. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: stable square-multiplication definition; PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: Section 3.1]
statement.algorithm_linkage: Equation (8) is a local reusable rule for a stable matrix-product call with inherited operand errors; it contains no triangular-matrix variables and is later reused in dense inversion. In Section 3.1 it is invoked twice for the off-diagonal inverse block, first for T11^(-1) T12 and then for (T11^(-1) T12) T22^(-1); that parenthesization is explicitly described as arbitrary. The complete recursive algorithm supplies the inherited errors and recurrence, but is not a prerequisite for the local rule itself. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8) and subsequent recurrences; PDF p. 10 (printed 68), anchor: later uses of equation (8)]
numerical_model: The only explicit local multiplication model is the aggregate normwise bound ||C_comp-C|| <= mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B|| + O(epsilon^2). [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1)]
Equation (8) retains only terms first order in fresh roundoff and inherited errors. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence and equation (8)]

The paper identifies epsilon as machine epsilon bounding roundoff but does not specify radix, rounding mode, scalar-operation formulas, fused operations, or a particular floating-point format in this setup. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: sentence defining epsilon; PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]

The enclosing Section 3 permits extra precision for logarithmic stability, but equation (8) itself uses a single generic working epsilon rather than a level-dependent precision schedule. [PDF pp. 6-7 (printed 64-65), anchor: logarithmic-stability setup and Lemma 3.2; PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]
error_notions: Equation (1) is a normwise forward error bound for a computed matrix product relative to the exact product. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1)]

Equation (8) is an absolute normwise first-order product-error rule, not a componentwise rule and not a relative-error formula. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: sentence calling err(T^(-1),n) absolute and equation (8)]

err(A,n) and err(B,n) are inherited operand-error magnitudes; err(C,n) accounts for both those propagated errors and new multiplication roundoff. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8) and its three annotations]
In the recursive application, err(n') is an upper bound uniform over the encountered diagonal inverse subblocks of order n'. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: definition of err(n')]

The resulting absolute inverse-error bound is converted into the surrounding claim of logarithmic stability by comparison with ||T^(-1)|| and kappa(T). [PDF p. 9 (printed 67), anchor: solved recurrence and concluding sentence]
norms: The norm in equations (1) and (8) and in Section 3.1 is deliberately not named as a specific matrix norm. The paper says norms can be exchanged using finite-dimensional norm equivalence, with added n-dependent factors. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: paragraph following equation (1)]

The propagation terms in equation (8) require a product-compatible submultiplicative norm and the triangle inequality; these properties are used implicitly rather than separately axiomatized. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]

The triangular proof explicitly relies on ||Tii|| <= ||T|| and ||Tii^(-1)|| <= ||T^(-1)|| because the blocks are submatrices. A formal norm choice must validate these inequalities or include replacement equivalence constants. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: paragraph after equation (8)]

The 2-norm is explicitly selected only later for the dense-inversion analysis; that later specialization does not retroactively identify the unnamed norm used in equation (8)'s triangular-inversion setting. [PDF p. 10 (printed 68), anchor: 'For the rest of this section the matrix norm ... will denote the 2-norm']

Changing the norm can change the effective dimension dependence of the multiplication bound and hence the exponent c absorbed into mu(n). [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: norm-equivalence discussion after equation (1)]
constants_and_indexing: mu(n)=O(n^c) for a constant c and is associated with the local multiplication dimension and chosen normwise stability bound. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: definition of mu(n)]
At a recursive level for an n-by-n T, each multiplication is on n/2-by-n/2 blocks and therefore uses mu(n/2), not mu(n). [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: recursive product-error inequalities]
Equation (8) has coefficient one on each of its three displayed first-order contributions; no additional constant or index offset is printed there. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]

The diagonal blocks are indexed T11 and T22, and the chosen multiplication order is T11^(-1) T12 followed by multiplication by T22^(-1). [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: block inverse formula and parenthesization note]
The recursive bound uses kappa(T)=||T|| ||T^(-1)|| and produces the factor [2(kappa(T)+1)]^(log_2 n). [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed 66-67), anchor: condition-number paragraph and solved recurrence]
higher_order_terms: Equation (1) explicitly includes an O(epsilon^2) remainder, whereas equation (8) suppresses that remainder under its stated first-order analysis. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence and equation (8)]

Writing computed operands as A+Delta A and B+Delta B shows that the omitted inherited-error cross term is Delta A Delta B, bounded by err(A,n) err(B,n). This omission is the algebraic first-order interpretation of the paper's setup rather than a term explicitly enumerated by the authors. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: inherited-error sentence and equation (8)]

Also omitted are corrections from evaluating the local multiplication-roundoff bound on perturbed operands, such as terms of scale epsilon ||A|| err(B,n), epsilon err(A,n) ||B||, and smaller products. These are second order when inherited errors are themselves first order in epsilon. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence and equation (8)]

Thus equation (8) is valid as the paper uses it only modulo quadratic and higher perturbation terms; without first-order scaling of inherited errors, the omitted cross terms need not be negligible. [PDF pp. 6 and 8 (printed 64 and 66), anchor: perturbative framework and first-order product analysis]
exceptional_values: No assumptions about overflow, underflow, subnormals, infinities, NaNs, or exceptional-operation behavior are stated in equation (1), equation (8), or the surrounding triangular-inversion analysis. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1) and epsilon definition; PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: Section 3.1 and equation (8)]
No radix, rounding direction, or concrete machine format is specified; machine epsilon is the only explicit machine parameter. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: sentence following equation (1)]

The product rule itself does not require invertible operands, but its triangular-inversion use presupposes that T and its diagonal blocks are invertible; singular-input behavior is not addressed. [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: block inverse formula]

undebatable_constraints: Equation (8) must retain all three displayed first-order terms: fresh multiplication error, propagated error from B, and propagated error from A. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]

The fresh multiplication term must be mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B|| and comes from the stable normwise multiplication assumption (1). [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first line of equation (8)]
The two inherited-error terms must be ||A|| err(B,n) and err(A,n) ||B||, with the operand roles and order shown. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: second and third lines of equation (8)]

The printed equality must not be interpreted as an exact identity of actual errors; the source explicitly places it in a first-order analysis and subsequently uses inequalities and bounds. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence and recurrences after equation (8)]
The rule is absolute and normwise, not relative or componentwise. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: absolute-error sentence and contrast with the stronger componentwise bound]
mu is polynomial in dimension and can acquire additional dimension dependence when the norm is changed. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: paragraph following equation (1)]

Equation (8) is a local product rule and does not require the complete recursive triangular-inversion algorithm, although that algorithm is the immediate application. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: generic product wording and recursive applications; PDF p. 10 (printed 68), anchor: reuse of equation (8)]

Cross products of inherited errors and all other quadratic or higher perturbation terms are outside the retained first-order contract. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence and equation (8)]

No exceptional-value or detailed floating-point-format contract may be attributed to this passage beyond the use of machine epsilon to bound roundoff. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: epsilon definition; PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]

ambiguities.issue: Formal status of the equality sign in equation (8)
ambiguities.evidence: The display uses '=', but the immediately preceding sentence calls the analysis first order, err(n') is later called a bound, and every concrete application is written with '<='. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8) and following recurrences]
ambiguities.impact: A formal contract should encode a first-order upper bound or equality modulo higher-order terms, not literal equality between the actual output-error norm and the displayed sum.

ambiguities.issue: Explicit scaling hypothesis for inherited operand errors
ambiguities.evidence: The source calls err(A,n) and err(B,n) inherited errors inside a first-order analysis but never separately states that each is O(epsilon). The recursive result is nevertheless linear in epsilon. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed 66-67), anchor: equation (8), recursive recurrences, and final bound]
ambiguities.impact: Treating inherited errors as first order is justified within the recursive perturbation argument, but equation (8) is not a complete bound for arbitrarily large inherited errors.

ambiguities.evidence: The source calls err(T^(-1),n) an absolute error, calls err(n') a bound, and uses err(A,n) and err(B,n) without defining whether they are exact error norms, selected upper bounds, or worst-case functions. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: paragraph containing equation (8)]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must choose a bound interpretation and should not infer an exact scalar error function beyond what the source supplies.

ambiguities.evidence: No norm is named in equations (1) or (8); norm equivalence is invoked generally, while the triangular proof assumes unit-constant submatrix inequalities. The 2-norm is selected only later. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: norm-equivalence discussion; PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: submatrix inequalities; PDF p. 10 (printed 68), anchor: later 2-norm specialization]
ambiguities.impact: The contract cannot quantify over arbitrary matrix norms without qualification; it needs compatible submultiplicativity and the stated submatrix behavior, or explicit equivalence constants.

ambiguities.evidence: The relevant definitions refer only to square and triangular matrices and do not say whether entries are real or complex. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: stable multiplication definition; PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: recursive triangular inversion]
ambiguities.impact: No real-only or complex-only restriction is source-mandated for this passage.

ambiguities.issue: Uniformity of big-O terms and smallness conditions
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (1) contains O(epsilon^2), and the paper allows polynomial n-factors in error notation, but it does not state uniform constants or a condition such as mu(n) epsilon < 1 in this passage. [PDF pp. 2-3 (printed 60-61), anchor: equation (1), mu definition, and O(epsilon) convention]
ambiguities.impact: The claim is asymptotic first-order error accounting, not a fully quantified finite-epsilon theorem with explicit thresholds.

ambiguities.issue: Recursive dimension parity and base case
ambiguities.evidence: Section 3.1 repeatedly partitions into n/2-by-n/2 blocks but does not state a power-of-two assumption, padding method, odd-size split, or scalar base-case error model. [PDF pp. 7-8 (printed 65-66), anchor: block inverse formula and dimension sentence]
ambiguities.impact: This omission affects a complete recursive-algorithm specification but not the local product rule in equation (8).

ambiguities.evidence: The setup defines epsilon only as machine epsilon bounding roundoff and supplies no overflow, underflow, special-value, radix, or rounding-mode assumptions. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: sentence following equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)]
ambiguities.impact: Such machine-format assumptions cannot be added to the source contract; implementations requiring them must state them separately.

contract_plain_english: Assume a stable normwise n-by-n multiplication routine satisfying equation (1). If its two input matrices already carry first-order absolute normwise errors, then equation (8) accounts for the computed product's first-order error by adding exactly three contributions: fresh multiplication roundoff mu(n) epsilon ||A|| ||B||, propagation of B's error through A, and propagation of A's error through B. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: equation (1); PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: equation (8)] The printed equality is first-order bound notation, not an exact identity: quadratic inherited-error products, interactions between inherited errors and new roundoff, and the O(epsilon^2) remainder are omitted. [PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: first-order-analysis sentence and subsequent inequalities] The rule is local and reusable; recursive triangular inversion applies it twice to -T11^(-1) T12 T22^(-1), using local dimension n/2, suitable norm properties, and inherited inverse errors to obtain its logarithmic-stability recurrence. [PDF pp. 8-9 (printed 66-67), anchor: recursive applications and solved recurrence] The norm and scalar domain are not fixed, mu may change with dimension and norm choice, and no machine assumptions beyond machine epsilon bounding roundoff are supplied. [PDF p. 2 (printed 60), anchor: mu, epsilon, and norm discussion; PDF p. 8 (printed 66), anchor: Section 3.1 error analysis]
